summary:
This evaluation covered 13 evals, with 4 "negative" evals (neg-s3-lifecycle, neg-bedrock-throttling, neg-cfn-authoring, neg-lambda-timeout) skipped entirely because they test should_trigger:false scenarios — both variants correctly did not trigger (6/6 each), but no other dimension was measured for these, so they contribute no comparative signal. The remaining 9 evals are chat-task automation scenarios (SSM runbook discovery/execution, hardening, diagnosis, approvals).

Across these 9 evals, a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met the expected output as often as or more often than without_skill in every eval except one (auto-find-ssh-unreachable, where both tied at 2/6). The gaps ranged from small (auto-find-public-bucket: 5/6 vs 5/6 tie on expected_output despite assertion differences; auto-run-diagnose-failure: 3/6 vs 2/6) to large (auto-find-account-fallback: 6/6 vs 1/6; auto-run-rate-control: 5/6 vs 1/6; auto-run-waiting-approval: 6/6 vs 5/6; auto-harden-vulnerable: 6/6 vs 3/6; auto-harden-clean: 6/6 vs 0/6). Per-assertion pass rates mirror this: with_skill matched or exceeded without_skill's assertion pass rate in every eval, sometimes substantially (e.g., auto-harden-clean 100% vs 67%, auto-run-waiting-approval 100% vs 40%, auto-find-public-bucket 47% vs 0%).

Several assertions passed for both variants (e.g., "does not search runbooks owned by other accounts," "reports no critical/high findings," "flags command-injection risk") — these are not discriminating and reflect shared strengths. Some assertions failed for both variants (e.g., "account-owned search filter is used," "step-level API is used," "child executions listed by parent") — these look like systematic gaps or possibly miscalibrated assertions/skill behavior rather than a variant-specific weakness. A few assertions showed a clean split where with_skill passed and without_skill failed consistently (e.g., send-automation-signal commands, documentation citations, timeoutSeconds handling) — these are the most discriminating data points and consistently favor with_skill.

On trigger_fired (measured once per eval, not per variant), rates varied by eval (33%–100%), reflecting how often the underlying behavior-under-test activated at all, independent of variant.

Quality comparisons (pairwise LLM judgments on accuracy/actionability/completeness) were only available for a subset of runs due to many skipped pairs (often 4-6 of 6 skipped). Where evaluated, most evals favored with_skill (e.g., auto-run-alarm-cancel: 10 vs 0; auto-run-waiting-approval: 14 vs 2; auto-run-rate-control and auto-run-diagnose-failure: 3 vs 0), but auto-harden-vulnerable showed the reverse (7 favoring without_skill vs 0 for with_skill, with high confidence) and auto-find-account-fallback leaned toward without_skill (3 vs 1) and auto-find-public-bucket was split evenly (2 vs 2). So quality judgments are not uniformly one-directional, and confidence on these ranged from medium to high with a meaningful share of pairs skipped, limiting how much weight they can carry.

On cost and runtime, without_skill was cheaper and/or faster in most evals (e.g., auto-harden-vulnerable: 23s/$0.19 vs 59s/$0.50; auto-find-account-fallback: 11s/$0.10 vs 32s/$0.27), while with_skill was occasionally faster/cheaper in a couple of cases (auto-find-public-bucket, auto-find-ssh-unreachable) and slightly slower in auto-run-alarm-cancel. None of the runtime thresholds were exceeded except one instance in auto-harden-vulnerable. So without_skill tends to run leaner, but this coincides with it meeting expected output and assertions less often in most evals — a speed/cost vs. completeness tradeoff rather than a clear win for either.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was mixed: without_skill was rated "consistent" (top score) in several evals (auto-run-waiting-approval, auto-harden-vulnerable, auto-harden-clean) but "inconsistent" in others (auto-run-diagnose-failure, auto-run-alarm-cancel). with_skill was mostly "mostly_consistent" across evals, with one "inconsistent" rating (auto-run-alarm-cancel) and no data for auto-find-ssh-unreachable. Neither variant was uniformly more stable.

Confidence levels on expected-output and assertion judgments were mostly medium-to-high, with no flagged low-confidence results, lending reasonable weight to the directional findings, though many quality-comparison pairs were skipped, and several assertions were flagged as "flaky" or "always fails," indicating some test items may not be reliably discriminating regardless of variant.

Overall, with_skill met expected outputs and individual assertions at least as often as without_skill in nearly every eval, often by a wide margin, while without_skill generally ran faster and cheaper and showed somewhat better run-to-run consistency in a few evals; quality judgments (where available) mostly but not uniformly favored with_skill, with one eval (auto-harden-vulnerable) favoring without_skill's quality despite with_skill's higher assertion pass rate there. This is a mixed picture with clear tradeoffs rather than a uniform outcome in either direction.

auto-find-ssh-unreachable.summary:
Both variants were evaluated on the same 6-scenario chat task, where the behavior under test (trigger_fired) only fired in 2 of 6 runs overall — meaning for 4 of 6 scenarios, there's no real data to judge either variant on since the triggering condition wasn't met. This caps how much confidence can be placed in any of the findings here.

Expected-output match was identical for both variants: 2/6 (33%). For with_skill this judgment was made with high confidence; for without_skill the same score was reached but with only medium confidence, so the equivalence on this headline metric is somewhat less certain for without_skill.

At the assertion level, with_skill passed more often overall (14/30, 47%) than without_skill (8/30, 27%). Looking at individual assertions:
- One assertion ("Says the runbook needs approval before running, and does not start an execution") passed equally for both (3/6 each) — this assertion doesn't differentiate the variants.
- One assertion ("A risk tier from the skill's vocabulary is used") also passed equally (5/6 each, regex-checked) — again not a differentiator, and both do reasonably well here.
- Three assertions showed a gap favoring with_skill: confirming the runbook via describe-document with version (2/6 vs 0/6), stating the risk tier with supporting calls (2/6 vs 0/6), and using describe-document to confirm the runbook (2/6 vs 0/6, regex-checked). All three are flagged as "flaky" patterns, meaning results varied across runs rather than being stable, so these gaps should be read as directional signals rather than firm conclusions.
- No assertion favored without_skill outright; the best without_skill achieved was parity with with_skill.

On runtime and cost, with_skill was faster (8s vs 11s) and cheaper ($0.07 vs $0.10) on average. Context window utilization was identical (4.8%, no compaction) for both.

Quality comparison data is absent: all 6 pairs were skipped, with zero pairs actually evaluated, so no quality-based judgment can be drawn between the variants.

Output consistency data is asymmetric: with_skill has no consistency data (null), while without_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.0, high confidence) across 3 dimensions. Since with_skill's consistency wasn't measured at all, no comparison can be made on this dimension — it's a gap in data, not a sign with_skill was inconsistent.

Overall state: the two variants tied on the highest-level expected-output metric (with slightly lower confidence for without_skill), but with_skill showed higher per-assertion pass rates, particularly on describe-document confirmation and risk-tier justification assertions, alongside faster and cheaper runs. However, these assertion-level gaps are all marked flaky (run-to-run variability), the trigger for the underlying behavior only fired in a third of scenarios, and quality/consistency comparisons are largely missing or one-sided, so the overall picture rests on a fairly thin and somewhat unstable evidence base rather than a clear, confident separation between the two variants.

auto-find-public-bucket.summary:
This chat-task eval covers a scenario involving confirming an SSM runbook in us-west-2, reporting its tier/version, and naming the API that sets the tier. A key contextual note: the overall "trigger_fired" rate was only 3/6 (50%), meaning the specific behavior under test only engaged in half of the runs for this scenario — so a sizable share of the data behind these numbers reflects runs where the behavior may not even have been exercised; that tempers confidence in all downstream findings.

Expected-output: both variants matched the expected output at the same rate, 5/6 (83%), with medium confidence and no low-confidence judgments. On this coarse measure, without_skill and with_skill are tied.

Per-assertion results (30 assertions each, 6 runs x 5 assertions): here the two variants diverge sharply. Variant_b passed 14/30 (47%) overall, while without_skill passed 0/30 (0%). Breaking down the five individual assertions, with_skill passed each one in 2-3 of 6 runs (33-50%), while without_skill failed every single instance of every assertion (0/6 on all five). All five assertions are flagged as "flaky" patterns, meaning even with_skill's passes were inconsistent run-to-run rather than reliable. So while with_skill did not reliably pass any assertion either, it did pass intermittently where without_skill did not pass at all. This is a notable and consistent split that the top-line "expected output" match-rate (tied at 83%) completely hides.

Quality comparison: only 2 of 6 pairs were evaluated (4 were skipped), so this is a thin sample. Within those 2 pairs, results were split evenly — 2 "with_skill favored", 2 "without_skill favored", 2 "comparable" across the overall tally, with per-criterion detail also mixed (accuracy split 1-1, actionability leaning with_skill, completeness leaning without_skill). Confidence on quality judgments is medium. With only two pairs assessed, this should be read as inconclusive rather than a meaningful signal in either direction.

Runtime and cost: without_skill ran faster on average (6s vs 9s) and cost slightly less ($0.06 vs $0.08). Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the 2 pairs evaluated. These are modest differences in absolute terms.

Output consistency: both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" overall. Variant_b scored slightly higher (2.33, with 1 "consistent" + 2 "mostly_consistent" dimension) versus without_skill (2.0, all 3 dimensions "mostly_consistent"), though without_skill's rating carries high confidence versus with_skill's medium confidence. The two are close, with a slight edge in consistency score for with_skill offset by slightly higher measurement confidence for without_skill.

Overall, the picture is mixed: the two variants tie on the aggregate expected-output match rate, but the detailed assertion-level data show with_skill achieving partial, flaky success on specific sub-criteria (naming the tier, the API, confirming the runbook, reporting version) that without_skill failed entirely across all runs. At the same time, without_skill was somewhat faster and cheaper, and the quality and consistency comparisons are both roughly even or too sparse (2/6 pairs) to draw firm conclusions. The low trigger-fire rate (50%) and the "flaky" labeling on every assertion suggest meaningful run-to-run variability underlies all of these numbers, so these findings should be treated as directional rather than definitive.

auto-find-account-fallback.summary:
This eval tested a chat task around searching for AWS Systems Manager runbooks. The trigger behavior under test fired in 5/6 runs (83%), so most runs produced usable data, but one run's trigger condition didn't fire — meaning not all 6 runs contributed cleanly to every measurement.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 6/6 runs (100%), while without_skill met it in only 1/6 runs (17%). Both measurements are backed by high confidence judgments, so this is a reasonably solid signal of a difference between the two variants on this specific criterion, not just noise.

Per-assertion detail (30 assertion checks per variant, grouped into 5 distinct assertion types):
- "Does not search or recommend runbooks owned by other accounts" passed 100% of the time for both variants — this assertion doesn't differentiate them.
- "The account-owned search filter is used" (regex-based) failed for both variants in all runs — this suggests either the behavior isn't implemented in either variant or the assertion itself may not be well-calibrated to the actual outputs.
- "Searches with list-documents using DocumentType=Automation and Owner=Self" passed 5/6 for with_skill but 0/6 for without_skill — a clear divergence.
- "Tries more than one keyword" passed 4/6 for with_skill vs 0/6 for without_skill — another clear divergence.
- "Says no AWS-owned runbook in the catalog fits before searching further" was weak for both (2/6 with_skill, 1/6 without_skill) and flagged as flaky — low reliability on this specific checkpoint for either variant.
Overall assertion pass rate was 57% for with_skill vs 23% for without_skill, driven mainly by the two assertions where without_skill failed consistently.

Quality comparison: only 1 of 6 pairs was actually evaluated for quality (5 were skipped), so this comes from a very small, low-coverage sample. Within that single evaluated pair, without_skill was favored more often across criteria (actionability, completeness) while accuracy was split 1-1, and the overall tally favored without_skill 3-to-1 against with_skill's 1. Given only one pair was assessed, this should be treated as a weak, low-coverage signal rather than a robust finding, and it stands in some tension with the expected-output results above, which favored with_skill.

Runtime and cost: without_skill ran faster (~11s vs ~32s) and cheaper (~$0.10 vs ~$0.27) on average. Neither variant exceeded the runtime threshold in the one evaluated pair. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (5.8% vs 6.8%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" across repeated runs, with identical overall scores (2.33) and identical dimension-count breakdowns (1 consistent, 2 mostly_consistent), both at high confidence — no meaningful difference in run-to-run stability between them.

Overall picture: with_skill more reliably met the expected output and passed more assertions, particularly around search behavior (DocumentType/Owner filter usage and trying multiple keywords), while without_skill was notably faster and cheaper and was favored in a very small, low-confidence quality sample. One assertion (other-account exclusion) passed universally and doesn't distinguish the two; another (account-owned filter regex check) failed universally and may indicate a gap or assertion-calibration issue affecting both. Consistency across runs was equivalent for both variants. The quality-comparison finding is the weakest piece of evidence here given its 1-of-6 coverage and should not be weighted as heavily as the expected-output and assertion results.

auto-harden-vulnerable.summary:
This eval tested a chat-based security review task (hardening an AWS Systems Manager document) across 6 runs per variant. The trigger behavior fired in all cases (6/6), so both variants were meaningfully exercised.

**Meeting expected output**: with_skill met the expected output in 6/6 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in only 3/6 runs (50%, medium confidence). This is a substantial and fairly well-supported gap.

**Assertions**: Across 72 total assertion checks, with_skill passed 100% (72/72) and without_skill passed 64% (46/72). Looking at the per-assertion breakdown is important because the aggregate hides a lot:
- Several assertions passed for both variants every time ("always_passes" pattern) — flagging the LogPath injection risk, the DbPassword secret exposure, curl -k disabling TLS, the hard-coded assumeRole ARN, returning a complete hardened YAML document, and absence of raw account IDs. These are not differentiating; both variants handle them reliably.
- Several assertions show a clear split where with_skill passed consistently and without_skill was flaky or failed outright: flagging SecureString as an invalid type (without_skill 1/6), flagging the 1200s timeout exceeding the 600s max (without_skill 2/6), flagging invalid onCancel routing (without_skill 5/6), citing documentation for findings (without_skill 0/6, the one case where with_skill and without_skill diverge completely — "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails"), the instance ID pattern being applied (without_skill 1/6), and lowering the executeScript timeout to 600 (without_skill 1/6). These specific checks are where the two variants genuinely diverge, with without_skill showing inconsistent/flaky behavior rather than uniform failure.

**Runtime and cost**: without_skill was notably faster (23s avg vs 59s avg) and cheaper ($0.19 vs $0.50 avg). One of three evaluated runtime pairs exceeded a 30s threshold. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.8% vs 5.7%), with no compaction for either.

**Quality comparison**: Only 3 of 6 pairs were evaluated for quality (3 skipped), which limits confidence somewhat, though the evaluated pairs carried high confidence. Among those, without_skill was favored in 7 of 9 criterion-level comparisons (all 3 accuracy comparisons and all 3 actionability comparisons favored without_skill), with 2 comparable and 0 favoring with_skill. This quality comparison is in tension with the expected-output and assertion results above, since without_skill performed worse on meeting expected output and much worse on assertions, yet was favored on the quality dimensions that were actually compared — though this quality signal rests on a small, partially-skipped sample (3 of 6 pairs).

**Output consistency**: without_skill was rated "consistent" across all three dimensions (score 3.0), while with_skill was "mostly_consistent" (score 2.33, with 1 consistent and 2 mostly-consistent dimension ratings). Both had high confidence in these ratings. So without_skill's outputs were somewhat more stable run-to-run on this specific consistency measure, even though its substantive correctness (expected output, assertions) varied more across runs.

**Overall picture**: There is a clear, well-supported divergence in correctness: with_skill reliably satisfied the expected output and all assertions, while without_skill was flaky on several specific security/validation checks (SecureString typing, timeout limits, onCancel routing, documentation citations, instance ID masking, and lowering the executeScript timeout). At the same time, without_skill ran faster and cheaper, and in the limited quality-comparison sample (half the pairs, high confidence) was rated more accurate and actionable, and was more internally consistent in its output style. These are competing signals rather than a single verdict: the assertion/expected-output data points to with_skill being more reliably correct on the specific technical checks tested, while the (partial) quality comparison and consistency rating point the other way, and the runtime/cost data favors without_skill's efficiency. Given the partial sample size for quality (3/6 pairs) and the medium confidence on without_skill's expected-output judgments, these findings should be weighed with some caution rather than treated as fully conclusive.
